description: Newton's three laws, F = ma calculations, inertial mass, weight versus mass, and stopping distances.
content_html:
Newton’s First Law

Newton’s First Law states that an object remains at rest or continues to move at constant velocity unless acted upon by a resultant force. This means:

• If the resultant force is zero, a stationary object stays still and a moving object keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
• If there is a resultant force, the object accelerates — which means it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction.

A spacecraft drifting in deep space continues at the same velocity indefinitely because there is no friction or air resistance to produce a resultant force. A book on a table remains stationary because the normal contact force from the table (upward) exactly balances its weight (downward).

Key Fact

Objects do not need a force to keep moving at constant velocity. A resultant force is only needed to change the speed or direction of an object. Zero resultant force → no change in motion.

Newton’s Second Law: F = ma

Newton’s Second Law states that the resultant force on an object is equal to its mass multiplied by its acceleration:

$$F = m \times a$$

Where \(F\) is resultant force (N), \(m\) is mass (kg), and \(a\) is acceleration (m/s²). The equation shows that a larger force produces a larger acceleration for the same mass, and a larger mass requires a larger force for the same acceleration. Remember: \(F\) is always the resultant force, not just any single force acting on the object.

Question: A car engine provides 4 200 N of driving force. Friction and air resistance total 1 400 N. The car has a mass of 700 kg. Calculate its acceleration.

Step 1: Find the resultant force: \(F = 4200 - 1400 = 2800 \text{ N}\)

Step 2: Apply Newton’s Second Law: \(a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{2800}{700} = 4 \text{ m/s}^2\)

You can investigate Newton’s Second Law using a trolley on a smooth track with a string passing over a pulley to a hanging mass. The hanging mass provides the driving force. Use light gates to measure acceleration. Keep the total mass of the system constant and vary the force by moving masses from the trolley to the hanger. Plot force against acceleration — a straight line through the origin confirms \(F \propto a\) at constant mass.

Weight, Mass and Gravitational Field Strength

Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It is measured in kg and does not change with location. Weight is the force of gravity acting on that mass, measured in newtons. The equation is:

$$W = m \times g$$

Where \(W\) is weight (N), \(m\) is mass (kg) and \(g\) is gravitational field strength (N/kg). At the Earth’s surface, \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\). A 70 kg person weighs 700 N on Earth but would weigh only about 112 N on the Moon, where \(g \approx 1.6 \text{ N/kg}\). Their mass stays at 70 kg in both locations. The numerical value of \(g\) at the Earth’s surface also equals the acceleration due to gravity in free fall (\(10 \text{ m/s}^2\)).

Inertial Mass

Inertial mass is defined as the ratio of the resultant force applied to an object to the acceleration it produces:

$$m = \frac{F}{a}$$

This is Newton’s Second Law rearranged. An object with greater inertial mass is harder to accelerate for the same applied force. Inertial mass and gravitational mass (the mass that determines how strongly gravity pulls an object) have the same value — this equivalence is a fundamental feature of physics and was central to Einstein’s thinking, though it is not required beyond GCSE level.

Newton’s Third Law

Newton’s Third Law states: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. These action-reaction pairs always act on different objects and are always the same type of force. For example:

• When you push a wall, the wall pushes back on you with an equal force in the opposite direction (both are normal contact forces).
• When the Earth pulls you downwards by gravity (your weight), you pull the Earth upwards with an equal gravitational force.
• A swimmer pushes water backwards — the water pushes the swimmer forwards.

A common mistake is to treat weight and the normal contact force as a Third Law pair. They are not — both act on the same object. A true Third Law pair involves forces on different objects.

Key Fact

Newton’s Third Law pairs: equal in size, opposite in direction, same type of force, acting on different objects. If both forces act on the same object, they are NOT a Third Law pair.

Stopping Distance

The total stopping distance of a vehicle is the sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance. Thinking distance is the distance covered from when the driver sees a hazard to when the brakes are applied. Braking distance is the distance covered while the brakes are applied and the vehicle slows to a stop.

• Factors increasing thinking distance: higher speed, tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions such as a mobile phone.
• Factors increasing braking distance: higher speed (braking distance is proportional to speed squared, so doubling speed quadruples braking distance), wet or icy roads, worn tyres, poorly maintained brakes, larger mass of vehicle.
• Speed affects both: at higher speed the vehicle covers more ground during the reaction time and also needs more braking distance to decelerate from a higher initial velocity.
exam_tip_html: For questions on stopping distance, always distinguish clearly between thinking distance and braking distance — examiners penalise conflating the two. For F = ma calculations, always work out the resultant force first before substituting; a common error is using the engine force alone when resistive forces are given. For Newton’s Third Law questions, check that your pair of forces acts on two different objects and is the same type of force — if both forces act on the same object, they are simply a balanced pair, not a Third Law pair.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Newton’s First Law: objects keep the same velocity unless a resultant force acts. Newton’s Second Law: \(F = ma\) where F is the resultant force. Newton’s Third Law: action-reaction forces are equal, opposite, same type, and act on different objects.
  • Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (\(W = mg\)). Mass is constant regardless of location; weight changes with gravitational field strength. On Earth, \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\).
  • Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Speed increases both. Reaction time affects thinking distance; road and vehicle conditions affect braking distance.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following describes Newton's First Law of motion?
A) Force equals mass times acceleration
B) Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
C) An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force
D) The rate of change of momentum equals the resultant force
practice_questions.marks: C) An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the equation that links weight, mass and gravitational field strength.
practice_questions.marks:
W = m × g [1 mark]
Where W = weight (N), m = mass (kg), g = gravitational field strength (N/kg).

practice_questions.text:
A shopping trolley of mass 25 kg experiences a pushing force of 80 N from a shopper and a friction force of 30 N opposing its motion.
Calculate the acceleration of the trolley.
practice_questions.marks:
Resultant force = 80 − 30 = 50 N [1 mark]
Apply F = ma: a = F ÷ m [1 mark]
a = 50 ÷ 25 = 2 m/s² [1 mark]
Unit: m/s² [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two factors that increase the thinking distance of a driver, and two factors that increase the braking distance of a vehicle.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for any two correct thinking distance factors: tiredness / alcohol / drugs / distraction (e.g. mobile phone) / higher speed. [1 mark]
One mark for any two correct braking distance factors: higher speed / wet or icy roads / worn tyres / faulty brakes / heavier vehicle. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A book rests on a table. Identify the Newton's Third Law pair to the weight of the book. Explain what makes these two forces a Third Law pair.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly identifies the reaction force — the gravitational pull of the book on the Earth (upward). States it is equal in size, opposite in direction, the same type of force (gravitational), and acts on the Earth (a different object). Distinguishes this from the normal contact force, which acts on the same object (the book) and is a different type of force. [3 marks]
Secure: Identifies reaction force and gives two of the four criteria. [2 marks]
Developing: Identifies 'the table pushing up' — this is the normal contact force, not the Third Law pair; gains no marks for identification but may gain 1 mark for criteria. [1 mark]
Emerging: Vague — 'the table pushes the book up' with no discussion of pairs. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'A heavier vehicle always has a longer stopping distance than a lighter vehicle travelling at the same speed.' Evaluate this statement, referring to both thinking distance and braking distance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Considers thinking distance (same for both vehicles at the same speed, as thinking distance depends on reaction time and speed, not mass). Evaluates braking distance (heavier vehicle stores more kinetic energy so needs greater braking force or longer distance to stop). Acknowledges that braking force also depends on road conditions and tyre quality — a heavier vehicle with better brakes or tyres may not necessarily stop in a longer distance. Reaches a justified conclusion with evidence from physics. [5–6 marks]
Secure: Correctly addresses braking distance, less detail on thinking distance, some reasoning. [3–4 marks]
Developing: States heavier = longer stopping distance without physics reasoning. [1–2 marks]
Emerging: Minimal physics content. [0 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: A car is travelling at constant velocity on a straight road. What must be true about the forces on the car?
options: There are no forces acting on the car
The driving force is greater than the resistive forces
The resistive forces are greater than the driving force

knowledge_checks.q: What is the weight of an object with a mass of 4 kg on Earth, where g = 10 N/kg?
Newton's Second Law states that the resultant force equals mass multiplied by _____.
Newton's Third Law pairs always act on _____ objects.
Match each Newton's Law to its correct description:
right: An object stays at rest or constant velocity unless a resultant force acts
For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction on a different object

flashcard_questions.a: An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.

flashcard_questions.q: State Newton's Second Law as an equation.

flashcard_questions.a: For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force acting on a different object.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
flashcard_questions.a: Mass is the amount of matter (kg, constant). Weight is the force of gravity on that mass (N, varies with g).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the value of g at the Earth's surface?
What is inertial mass defined as?
flashcard_questions.a: The ratio of resultant force to acceleration: m = F ÷ a.

flashcard_questions.q: What two distances make up the total stopping distance of a vehicle?
Give two factors that increase thinking distance.
flashcard_questions.a: Tiredness or alcohol (also: drugs, distractions, higher speed).

flashcard_questions.q: Give two factors that increase braking distance.
flashcard_questions.a: Wet roads and worn tyres (also: higher speed, heavier vehicle, faulty brakes).

flashcard_questions.q: A 50 kg object is on the Moon where g = 1.6 N/kg. What is its weight?
Why is weight and the normal contact force not a Newton's Third Law pair?
flashcard_questions.a: Both forces act on the same object — Third Law pairs act on different objects.

glossary_terms.definition: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion continues at the same speed and direction, unless acted on by an unbalanced (resultant) force.
The overall force on an object when all individual forces are combined, taking into account their direction.
The resultant force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration: F = ma.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg). Mass does not change with location.
The force of gravity acting on an object, measured in newtons (N). Weight depends on mass and gravitational field strength.
A measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object, defined as the ratio of resultant force to acceleration: m = F ÷ a.
For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force, acting on a different object.
